rationale: B wins because it behaves like an editor, not an angle vending machine: "Without the first item, do not pitch this angle" is exactly the discipline this update needs. A has strong raw material, but "On's circular-shoe expansion raises the question: does the rest of the running category have to follow?" stretches one national rollout into category pressure before the evidence earns it. B keeps four clean shapes and makes the missing proof part of the strategy instead of decorating around it.
gaps_in_A: "moving a core product line to this model" is not in the update. Cyclon may be important, but "core product line" is an invented upgrade.
"does the rest of the running category have to follow?" overstates the competitive implication. One fast-growing brand rolling out a subscription is not proof that incumbents are under pressure.

"The unlikely material behind On's shoe-recycling bet: castor beans" is plausible, but thin as a standalone angle from one supplied fact. It needs a hard gate: composition, sourcing, performance, and recyclability data first.
"Pick one angle, then use `find-journalists`" is premature. The founder needs recycling rate, price, pilot results, and geography before building lists.
gaps_in_B: "people who have already done a full cycle" assumes the pilot produced named full-cycle subscribers. The proof section catches this, but the angle body states it too confidently.
"sneaker company" is loose. On is supplied as an athletic/running brand; the safer beat language is running shoes or athletic footwear.
B underplays the possible materials-science story. The "castor-bean-based material" could justify its own manufacturing or bio-based feedstock angle if On can prove composition and performance.
